title: Namespace slicing and sticky routing demo - Pioneer Logistics
header: Date: 2027-11-29 | Start: 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~62m | Location: Zoom | Recording: yes | Deck: shared (link)
summary: Demo focused on namespace slicing, sticky routing and org/project key strategy to support Pioneer Logistics' multi-tenant inference workloads. Covered console walk-through, API key patterns, quota shapes (concurrency, token), and tradeoffs for hosted vs dedicated and private deployments. Agreed to run a short pilot with benchmark harness and trial project keys.
topics: namespace-slicing; sticky-routing; org vs project keys; quota shapes; burst capacity; fairshare; concurrency limits; dedicated vs hosted; security (SSO/SAML, KMS); next steps for POC
action_items: Avery Chen: Share pricing spreadsheet and dedicated capacity SKUs; due 2027-12-02
Marcus Patel: Prep benchmark test plan and sample load scripts (traffic patterns from Pioneer); due 2027-12-06
Alex Rivera: Provide representative traffic profile and top 20 endpoints; due 2027-12-03
Priya Nair: Identify stakeholders for pilot sign-off and required SSO attributes; due 2027-12-07
next_steps: Redwood to provision trial project keys and namespace slices for Pioneer
Schedule 60m POC kickoff (benchmarks + success criteria) next week
Send SOC2 / security one-pager and KMS integration notes
Follow up pricing for 3-month reserved burst capacity
transcript_body:
[00:00:05] Avery (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — from Redwood it's Avery and Marcus. Quick roll call?
[00:00:14] Alex (Pioneer CTO): Alex here, Priya and Sam from our infra team are on.
[00:00:18] Priya (Pioneer Eng Mgr): hi all.
[00:00:24] Marcus (Redwood SE): Great. Today we're going to demo namespace slicing and sticky-routing patterns — how you can map org/project keys to tenant slices, shape quotas and protect noisy tenants without impacting tail latency for others.
[00:00:37] Sam (SRE): we're especially worried about bursty traffic from our route planner and the last-mile ETA service — they spike and flatten other pipelines.
[00:00:45] Avery: Perfect, that's exactly what these patterns address. We'll start in the Console, then switch to the API and show how Optimize recommendations help pick batch sizes and quant profiles.
[00:00:58] Marcus: jumping in — console, top-left. Here's a customer with multiple projects: Production, Partners, Internal. You can see project-level keys mapped into namespaces (we call them slices) — each slice gets its own quota and concurrency budget.
[00:01:12] [00:01:18] Speaker 2 (auto): uh the console loads a little slowly for me — sorry.
[00:01:21] Marcus: no worries. Notice the sticky routing toggle — when on, requests from a project key will prefer the same serving pool (vCPU/GPU pool) to keep KV cache warm; if that pool is constrained the system will gracefully failover to a compatible variant.
[00:01:36] Priya: sticky routing sounds like it could create hotspots, though — how do you avoid one tenant monopolizing a GPU?
[00:01:43] Marcus: great question. We combine sticky routing with a fairshare allocator and per-slice hard caps. There are two controls: a soft concurrency floor and a hard concurrency cap. The allocator ensures long tail tasks can't evict other tenants; if a slice hits its hard cap we either queue or route to a lower-cost model variant depending on your policy.
[00:01:58] Alex: ah ok — so we could route the route-planner spikes to a cheaper quantized variant while preserving latency for high-priority flows?
[00:02:05] Marcus: Exactly. And Optimize can suggest which model variants to fallback to based on your latency SLO and historical token distribution.
[00:02:12] [00:02:30] Sam: on quota shapes, we run a mix of short high-QPS calls and long context requests. Can we set per-route token quotas vs concurrency quotas?
[00:02:38] Avery: yes — you can set per-route and per-project token quotas, and a separate concurrency quota. For example, put a per-route token cap on the big-context summarizer and a concurrency cap on the streaming endpoints.
[00:02:50] Marcus: additionally we have burst windows — short-time bursting that allows sudden surges within a time window, then reverts to baseline. That helps for traffic like nightly batch kicks or flash events.
[00:03:02] Priya: what's the billing implication during bursts? We don't want runaway costs.
[00:03:06] Avery: bursts consume quota units as usual; you can throttle cost by combining burst policies with budget guards — a checkout guard that blocks traffic when projected monthly spend exceeds threshold. We also expose token-level cost estimates in the console.
[00:03:20] Alex: Security — can we tie these project keys to our SSO groups and enforce RBAC? We need audit logs and KMS integration.
[00:03:27] Marcus: Yes. SSO via SAML/Okta maps to org and project roles; we support RBAC at the project slice level. Audit logs are shipped to your SIEM and we support customer-managed KMS for key encryption in Private deployments.
[00:03:42] [00:03:50] Speaker 1 (auto): i'm seeing small transcription errors, ignore me.
[00:03:54] Priya: Regarding private deployment — if we went that route could we still use the same console and APIs?
[00:03:59] Avery: The control plane is customizable. With Private (VPC/on-prem) you get a customer-manageable control plane and the same API surface; the console can be self-hosted or accessed via a private endpoint. We'll provide connectivity patterns for your network team.
[00:04:12] Marcus: For dedicated capacity, you get reserved GPU pools mapped to slices. That gives predictable latency and throughput, and you can pin critical slices to dedicated pools while keeping others on shared hosted capacity.
[00:04:23] Sam: How do you handle failover if a dedicated pool is down? We need graceful degradation, not total outage.
[00:04:29] Marcus: we have automatic fallback policies — canary to shared pools or lower-cost variants. You control the policy: immediate fallback, queue-then-fallback, or fail-open depending on tolerance.
[00:04:39] Alex: can we test multi-tenant interference?
[00:04:41] Marcus: yes — we'll run interference benchmarks in the POC: mix heavy KV-cache warming traffic with small infer requests to validate latency isolation.
[00:04:50] [00:05:05] Avery: switching to the API quickly. Here is a project key create call, you can set attributes: slice_id, quota_name, max_concurrency, burst_window_seconds, cost_center tag.
[00:05:17] Marcus: note the header-based key usage — you can use the same key across services; routing is decided by the slice mapping. If you rotate keys, we maintain sticky routing for existing sessions for a short handover period to avoid cold starts.
[00:05:30] Priya: about sticky routing and cold starts — does the system warm KV caches proactively?
[00:05:34] Marcus: We do prefetch heuristics and sticky affinity. For frequently accessed prefixes the runtime will keep KV in memory and prefer the same host. Optimize can recommend warm-up batch sizes to minimize latency without wasting tokens.
[00:05:46] Alex: What telemetry will we get during the POC? We need per-project token counts, per-route p50/p95 latency, concurrency graphs, and error traces.
[00:05:55] Avery: All exposed in the console and via APIs. We can stream traces to your APM and provide CSV exports for billing reconciliation.
[00:06:05] [00:06:40] Sam: our compliance team will want SOC2 artifacts and an architecture diagram showing data flows.
[00:06:45] Avery: We'll send the SOC2 pack and a recommended architecture diagram for Private deployment. Also include KMS/HSM notes.
[00:06:52] Priya: one more — can quotas be set at organization level with overrides at project level? We want org-wide cost guardrails but project-level flexibility.
[00:07:00] Marcus: yes — hierarchical quotas. Org quota sets the ceiling; projects inherit but can have tighter settings. We also support per-route overrides and temporary exemptions for partners.
[00:07:12] Alex: Any gotchas around API key hierarchy? We're concerned about keys proliferating.
[00:07:18] Marcus: We recommend a naming and lifecycle policy: org-level master key for infra automation, project-level keys for services, rotated monthly. The Console has a key inventory view to see last-used and usage spikes.
[00:07:30] [00:07:45] Avery: we'll run a quick demo of a throttle event. I'm going to throttle the Partners slice to a low concurrency cap... you should see error 429s for that project while Production flows continue.
[00:07:55] Speaker 3 (Jillian, Product): i get a 429 in my window. yep.
[00:08:00] Marcus: exactly — and the console shows detailed breakdown: which route, which key, token counts and minutes until quota reset. You can set webhook alerts or automatic ticket creation for ops.
[00:08:12] Priya: can we set per-route backpressure so streaming clients get notified gracefully?
[00:08:16] Marcus: yes — you can choose to stream a soft signal before 429, or send structured error with retry-after header and a suggested degraded model variant.
[00:08:26] Alex: How long does it take to spin up a dedicated pool? We might want burst capacity for peak end of quarter.
[00:08:30] Avery: Dedicated pools are booked monthly; for short-term bursts we recommend reserved burst capacity which can be turned on in minutes if within your committed envelope, or use hosted burst if latency tolerance is higher.
[00:08:42] Sam: ok. For the POC, we'll want three slices: Production (priority), Partners (partner integrations), and Experiments (low-priority). Production gets reserved pool, Partners gets burstable slice with hard token cap, Experiments on shared.
[00:08:55] Marcus: Good plan. We'll configure sticky routing for Production to keep caches warm.
[00:09:01] [00:09:34] (demo continues — Marcus shows API logs, sticky mapping table, quota timeline visualization)
[00:10:05] Priya: small nit: is there a way to auto-scale concurrency caps based on seasonality signals?
[00:10:10] Marcus: yes — autoscale policies can increase soft caps when average utilization crosses thresholds; you can also tie autoscale to calendar events or external signals via webhooks.
[00:10:20] Alex: great. Any restrictions on model variants across private/dedicated/hosted? We want the same model family everywhere.
[00:10:25] Marcus: Most open models are available across environments; quantized variants might differ by hardware. The runtime abstracts the variant so your API calls can stay the same; we recommend pinning model versions in production rollouts.
[00:10:36] Avery: wrapping up — recap: Redwood will provision trial keys and three slices, run interference benchmarks, send pricing & SOC2 docs. Pioneer provides traffic profile and stakeholder list.
[00:10:48] Alex: sounds good. Any final questions?
[00:10:51] Priya: can you include an example IaC snippet for creating slices? That would help our infra team.
[00:10:55] Marcus: yes we'll include Terraform and curl examples.
[00:11:02] Avery: Next meeting: 60m POC kickoff — propose 2027-12-07 17:00 UTC. We'll send a calendar invite. Thanks everyone.
[00:11:12] (call ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-attribution and small words missing; technical sections may have abbreviated terms (KV, SLO, RBAC).
